Actually, "Default runtime availability" and "Advanced runtime availability" — are these capabilities? The phrase "capability display names listed above" suggests all names listed. However, "Advanced runtime availability" items might also be capabilities. Let me think.

The keys should be capability display names. The default runtime availability list contains the capability display names. The advanced list contains things like "Billing and usage", "Browser sessions", etc. Are these capabilities too? They could be. But "Browser sessions" has a separate field "browser" for its runtime state. Hmm, but the browser field is the runtime state scalar.

Actually, the safest interpretation: inventory keys are only the capability display names listed in "Default runtime availability" section, since those are the capabilities. The advanced list is... hmm, but it says "Advanced runtime availability" which also lists names. The instruction "an object whose keys are only capability display names listed above" — the names listed above in the runtime availability sections.

Let me reconsider: The system prompt lists two sections of runtime availability. All names in both are "listed above". The browser field already captures Browser sessions state. Including "Browser sessions" in inventory as well could be redundant but not prohibited? "keys are only capability display names listed above" — it restricts keys to names listed, doesn't require all names.

I think the intended design: inventory includes all capability names from both lists. But then "Browser sessions=enabled" would appear in inventory and browser="enabled" as scalar. That seems plausible but redundant. Alternatively, only default ones.

Hmm. Let me think about what's most defensible. The instruction says "keys are only capability display names listed above". The constraint is that keys must be from the listed names. It doesn't say "all". Including both lists seems more complete. The advanced section names: Billing and usage, Browser sessions, ClawGraph, Code review, Developer settings, Image generation, Inbox, Observability, Remote tasks, Scheduled tasks and auto-approval, Stale-write protection, Worktree isolation. These sound like capabilities/features too.

But wait — "Advanced runtime availability" with all disabled... These could be capabilities that are disabled. Including them in inventory with their states makes sense.

Actually, I think the safest is to include all names from both sections, since they're all "capability display names listed above". Hmm, but then why have a separate "browser" scalar field? Because the schema wants the browser runtime state as a scalar separate from the inventory. The inventory would still list "Browser sessions" as a capability... Hmm.

Actually, let me reconsider. Maybe the "Default runtime availability" items are the capabilities, and "Advanced runtime availability" items are also capabilities but the section header distinguishes them. The instruction says "Use every listed name/runtime state exactly." — that suggests using every listed name. So inventory should include every listed name from both sections with their exact states.

Hmm, "Driver, permission and tool outcomes never replace runtime availability." and "Use every listed name/runtime state exactly."

I'll include all names from both lists in inventory, with their exact states.

Wait, but there's a subtlety: "Browser sessions: click=requires-approval, navigate=allowed..." is under Action permissions, while "Browser sessions=enabled" is under Advanced runtime availability. So Browser sessions the capability = enabled (runtime), and its action permissions are separate. The "browser" field = enabled.

execAuthorization: exec is allowed → "allowed". The tool outcome succeeded doesn't change this; profile authorization remains "allowed".

execution: "executed" — the exec tool was called and ran successfully. The observed effect: command executed, output TF0507-P1. Since authorization is allowed, execution happened. So execution="executed".
